source.version: Published journal article (Original Research), Frontiers in Psychology 16:1508383, published 02 July 2025; DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1508383 (p. 1).
source.title_on_document: EEG assessment of artificial intelligence-generated content impact on student creative performance and neurophysiological states in product design

supplement.holds: Not stated: the PDF links supplementary material but does not identify its contents or any supplement-only statistics. It is not appended to this PDF. The main PDF contains the creative-performance arm means, SDs and counts (p. 8, Table 1), raw difference and confidence interval (p. 9, Table 2), and Cohen’s d (p. 11, section 4.1).

paper_design_summary: In a controlled university design laboratory, undergraduate design students were explicitly described as randomly assigned to AIGC-assisted design or conventional design tools, although the research-design paragraph also calls the study quasi-experimental (p. 4, sections 3.1 and 3.2). Students designed an intelligent walking cane using AI dialogue and image generation or internet research and conventional design software, and design experts rated the submitted work using the Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale (pp. 5–6, sections 3.2.3, 3.3.1 and 3.4). EEG monitoring and interviews accompanied this single experiment but did not score creative outputs.

studies.label: Intelligent walking cane design: AIGC versus traditional design tools

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were assigned to the AIGC experimental group or the traditional-software control group. Cluster random sampling describes recruitment; the subsequent assignment statement refers to participants. The experiment took place in a controlled multimedia classroom at the Design Innovation Laboratory, with conditions in separate rooms. The explicit random-assignment statement supports lab_rct despite the conflicting quasi-experimental label.
assignment.quote: They were randomly assigned to either the experimental group (n = 32; 17 females, 15 males) or the control group (n = 32; 16 females, 16 males).
assignment.locator: p. 4, section 3.1 Participants (random assignment and recruitment); p. 4, section 3.2.1 Research variables (quasi-experimental label); p. 4, section 3.2.2 Equipment (controlled laboratory); p. 5, section 3.2.3 Research procedure (separate rooms).

arms.name: Experimental group (AIGC)
arms.description: ChatGPT, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion were provided as AIGC tools. The described workflow uses ChatGPT for concept exploration, Stable Diffusion for images, and Photoshop or Illustrator for post-processing (p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 6, section 3.4.2). Assignment counts: p. 4, section 3.1; analyzed counts: p. 8, Table 1.

arms.name: Control group (traditional tools)
arms.description: No AIGC assistance. Participants researched literature and existing products on the internet, sketched, modeled and rendered designs, and used conventional software including Photoshop, Illustrator, Rhinoceros, KeyShot and Autodesk Maya (p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 6, section 3.4.3). Coded other_aid because the comparison includes internet research and conventional design aids. Assignment counts: p. 4, section 3.1; analyzed counts: p. 8, Table 1.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition are reported. Table 1 analyzes 32 students per arm, matching the assignment counts in section 3.1; no intention-to-treat designation is stated (p. 4, section 3.1; p. 8, Table 1).
participants.who: Third-year undergraduate students from Product Design and Visual Communication Design programs at a public university in Eastern China, enrolled in a Design Innovation course. Participants had foundational design and software training but no prior formal AIGC design training (p. 4, section 3.1).
participants.quote: The study included a total of 64 participants, with 32 in the experimental group and 32 in the control group.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 3.1 Participants (sample and randomized arm counts); p. 7, section 3.7 Quantitative analysis results (quoted analyzed sample); p. 8, Table 1 (32 analyzed per arm, total 64).

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion; model versions not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Combined dialogue and image-generation workflow: participants used multiple rounds of ChatGPT dialogue for concepts, functions, interaction methods and optimization suggestions, then generated design images with Stable Diffusion and adjusted generation parameters. Midjourney is also listed among the available tools. Photoshop or Illustrator supported post-processing. The role field records image generation; open-ended chatbot ideation was also part of the intervention (p. 4, section 3.2.2; p. 6, section 3.4.2).

task.description: Design an intelligent walking cane for elderly people or people with mobility impairments, incorporating functionality, intelligent features, ergonomics, aesthetics, innovation and durability. Required deliverables were design sketches, three-dimensional models and rendered images (p. 6, section 3.4.1).
task.duration: 3 h for the design task (p. 6, section 3.4.1).

outcomes.name: Creative performance (Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale composite)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three design-field experts independently scored the submitted work using the 30-item Creative Solution Diagnosis Scale (CSDS). Items use ratings from 1 to 5, with a possible total of 150 and higher scores indicating better creative performance. The dimensions are Relevance and Effectiveness, Novelty, Elegance, and Genesis. The methods describe weighted dimension scores, but only aggregate creative-performance results are reported; the dimensions are included here as components, not separate reported outcomes. The exact aggregation across raters and rater blinding are not stated. The analysis uses participant-level creative-performance scores (pp. 5–6, section 3.3.1; p. 7, section 3.6; p. 8, Table 1).

contrasts.reported: Experimental group: Mean = 115.13, Std. Deviation = 6.440, N = 32; Control group: Mean = 110.69, Std. Deviation = 9.372, N = 32 (Table 1). Mean difference = 4.438; 95% confidence interval of difference: Lower = 0.419, Upper = 8.456; Sig. (2-tailed) = 0.031 (Table 2). Prose reports t(62) = 2.208, p = 0.031, Cohen’s d = 0.55. The confidence interval concerns the raw mean difference, not d. Table 2 has the t and df column headings transposed; the test is labeled here according to the prose.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 1 (means, SDs, analyzed counts) and section 3.7 (t and p); p. 9, Table 2 (mean difference, confidence interval and p); p. 11, section 4.1 (t, p and Cohen’s d).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No shared participants or reanalysis of another paper’s sample is reported; the methods describe recruitment for this study.

company_involvement.description: No specific company or AI-tool provider is stated to be involved. Authors have educational-institution affiliations. Funding includes educational and institutional programs, including a university-industry/academic-research fund, but no specific company is named. The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could constitute a conflict of interest.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations; p. 14, Funding and Conflict of interest.

eligibility.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly states random assignment of students to AIGC versus traditional-tool conditions (p. 4), despite the conflicting quasi-experimental label in section 3.2.1 on the same page. This is coded lab_rct based on that allocation statement and the controlled Design Innovation Laboratory setting (p. 4, section 3.2.2). The analysis includes 64 people, 32 per arm (p. 7, section 3.7; p. 8, Table 1). Design experts scored participants’ creative work using CSDS (pp. 5–6, sections 3.2.3 and 3.3.1), and AI was used during production of the scored design (p. 6, section 3.4.2). The no-AIGC control used internet research and conventional design aids, coded ai_vs_active (p. 6, section 3.4.3).

one_line_finding: Among 64 analyzed design students, AIGC-assisted designs received higher CSDS creative-performance scores than traditional-tool designs (M = 115.13, SD = 6.440 versus M = 110.69, SD = 9.372; p. 8, Table 1), with t(62) = 2.208, p = 0.031 and Cohen’s d = 0.55 (p. 11, section 4.1).
open_questions: Why does section 3.2.1 call the design quasi-experimental despite the explicit random-assignment statement in section 3.1? The allocation-sequence method is not described (p. 4).
What does the online supplement contain? The PDF provides a link but no inventory or description of supplement-only statistics (p. 14, Supplementary material).
How were independent expert ratings combined into each participant’s CSDS score, and were the experts blinded to treatment? These details are not stated (pp. 5–6, section 3.3.1).
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. Read the complete markdown through the references; this PDF has no appended supplement. Checked PDF pages for publication details, design, assignment and participant counts, task, scoring, Tables 1 and 2, reported Cohen’s d, and disclosure/supplement statements. Table 2 visibly prints df above 2.208 and t above 62; the prose consistently reports t(62) = 2.208 (p. 8, section 3.7; p. 11, section 4.1), so its labels are used without calculating or replacing any statistics. Only the aggregate CSDS score has separately reported creative-output results; its dimensions are described in measure_detail. EEG concentration and relaxation, interviews, and correlations with physiological states are omitted because they do not add creative-output outcomes answering the atlas questions. No across-person diversity measure or later unassisted creative output is reported. Ratings occurred after task completion but concern designs produced with AI available, so the outcome is with_ai, not after_ai (pp. 5–6, sections 3.2.3 and 3.4.2). No preregistration or explicit primary-outcome designation is reported. The data-availability statement refers to the article/Supplementary material and inquiries to the corresponding author, without a separate data or code URL (p. 14).
